1. Introduction

This report documents the step-by-step process of setting up a small university-style network in VirtualBox. The lab combines four core Windows/Linux server administration skills into one exercise: Active Directory (identity and domain control), a Linux web server (Nginx), a Linux proxy server (Squid) that filters and logs web traffic, and DNS integration so the whole setup behaves like a real campus network.

The end goal is a working environment where a domain-joined client (CLIENT1) logs in with an Active Directory account, resolves an internal website by name using the domain's own DNS server, and only reaches that website (and the rest of the internet) through a proxy server that can allow, block, and log traffic.

2. Lab Objectives

Set up an isolated virtual network in VirtualBox (Internal Network)

Install and configure Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) on a Windows Server VM

Deploy a Linux web server using Nginx

Install and configure a Squid proxy server

Integrate proxy access with the domain network

Apply web access control (allow/deny) policies on the proxy

Test and troubleshoot DNS, web, and proxy connectivity

Part 1: Configure the Domain Controller (DC1)

DC1 is the heart of the network. It will hold Active Directory (user accounts and domain policy) and act as the DNS server for every other machine.

Step 1 – Set a Static IP Address

On DC1, open Network Settings for the LabNet adapter and configure:

IP Address: 192.168.10.10

Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.0

Default Gateway: 192.168.10.1

Preferred DNS: localhost

Step 2 – Install Active Directory Domain Services

Step 1: Open Server Manager.

Step 2: Click "Add Roles and Features".

Step 3: Proceed through the wizard and tick "Active Directory Domain Services".

Step 4: Click Install and wait for the role to finish installing.

Step 3 – Promote DC1 to a Domain Controller

Step 1: In Server Manager, click the notification flag and choose "Promote this server to a domain controller".

Step 2: Select "Add a new forest".

Step 3: Enter the root domain name: university.local

Step 4: Set a Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) password, accept the default DNS/NetBIOS options, and complete the wizard.

Step 5: Let the server reboot to finish promotion.

Step 4 – Create Domain User Accounts

Open Active Directory Users and Computers (ADUC) and create the following accounts under an appropriate OU (or the default Users container):

student1

Lecturer1

Part 2: Configure the Web Server (WEB1)

WEB1 will host a simple internal webpage — the "University Intranet Portal" — which stands in for a real internal application that students and staff would access.

Step 1 – Set a Static IP

IP Address: 192.168.10.20

DNS Server: 192.168.10.10

sudo nano /etc/netplan/00-installer-config.yaml
sudo netplan apply

Step 2 – Install Nginx

sudo apt update
sudo apt install nginx

Port 80

Step 3 – Create the Web Page

sudo nano /var/www/html/index.html

Replace the default content with:

<h1>University Intranet Portal</h1>

Save the file (Ctrl+O, Enter) and exit (Ctrl+X).

Step 4 – Test the Web Server

This is tested from a browser later (Part 6), but you can do a quick local check on WEB1 itself first:

curl http://localhost

Part 3: Configure DNS (on DC1)

Active Directory installs a DNS server automatically. We now add a friendly name for the intranet portal so users can browse to it by name instead of typing its IP address.

Step 1 – Open DNS Manager

On DC1: Server Manager → Tools → DNS.

Step 2 – Add an A Record

Inside the university.local forward lookup zone, add a new host (A) record:

Name

IP Address

portal

192.168.10.20

Step 3 – Test DNS Resolution

From CLIENT1 (once it is on the domain network), run:

nslookup portal.university.local

Part 4: Configure the Proxy Server (PROXY1)

PROXY1 uses Squid, a widely-used open-source proxy, to sit between clients and the internet/intranet. All web requests will be routed through it so traffic can be filtered and logged.

Step 1 – Set a Static IP

IP Address: 192.168.10.30

DNS Server: 192.168.10.10

sudo nano /etc/netplan/00-installer-config.yaml
sudo netplan apply
ip a

Step 2 – Install Squid

sudo apt update
sudo apt install squid

Step 3 – Configure Basic Proxy Access

sudo nano /etc/squid/squid.conf

Add the following lines (placed above the default "http_access deny all" line so they take effect):

acl localnet src 192.168.10.0/24
http_access allow localnet

Step 4 – Restart the Squid Service

sudo systemctl restart squid
sudo systemctl status squid

Ping DNS(DC1)

Part 5: Configure the Client (CLIENT1)

Step 1 – Set Networking to DHCP

Confirm CLIENT1's network adapter is set to "Obtain an IP address automatically" and "Obtain DNS server address automatically" (or manually point DNS to 192.168.10.10 if DHCP scope options are not configured on DC1).

Output of 'ipconfig /all' on CLIENT1 showing it received an address in the 192.168.10.0/24 range and DNS server 192.168.10.10.

Step 2 – Join the Domain

Step 1: Open System Properties → Change settings → Computer Name tab → Change…

Step 2: Select "Domain" and type: university.local

Step 3: When prompted, authenticate with a domain admin account (e.g. Administrator@university.local).

Step 4: Accept the welcome message and restart the computer.

Step 3 – Log In With a Domain Account

At the Windows login screen, sign in as:

university\student1

Part 6: Configure Browser Proxy Settings (on CLIENT1)

Step 1 – Open Browser/Windows Proxy Settings

Go to Settings → Network & Internet → Proxy (this also applies to most browsers that follow the system proxy).

Step 2 – Set the Proxy Address and Port

Proxy IP: 192.168.10.30

Port: 3128 (Squid's default listening port)

Step 3 – Test Proxy Access to the Portal

With the proxy enabled, browse to:

http://portal.university.local

The page should load and display "University Intranet Portal", confirming that DNS, the web server, and the proxy are all working together correctly.

5. Troubleshooting Guide

Problem

Likely Cause / Solution

Cannot join domain

Check that the client's DNS points to 192.168.10.10 (DC1). Domain join fails almost every time if DNS is wrong, since the client can't find the domain controller.

Website not loading

Check that Nginx is running on WEB1 (systemctl status nginx) and that the firewall isn't blocking port 80.

Proxy not working

Restart Squid (systemctl restart squid) and re-check squid.conf for syntax errors with squid -k parse.

DNS fails

Verify DC1's IP hasn't changed, the DNS service is running, and the A record for 'portal' exists in the university.local zone.

No connectivity between VMs

Confirm all four VMs are attached to the same VirtualBox Internal Network (LabNet), and that static IPs don't conflict.

7. Conclusion

This lab combined four previously separate skills, Active Directory, DNS, web hosting, and proxy administration into a single working network. It showed how these services depend on each other in a real environment: domain join fails without correct DNS, the friendly URL (portal.university.local) only works because DC1's DNS zone has an A record pointing at WEB1, and every client request only reaches the portal (or the wider internet) because it is routed through PROXY1 first.

The access-control step (Part 7) demonstrated how organizations enforce acceptable-use policy at the network level rather than on individual machines blocking a domain on the proxy affects every device that uses it, without needing to touch each computer separately. The logging step (Part 8) showed why proxies are also useful for auditing and troubleshooting: every request is timestamped and tied to a client IP, which is exactly the kind of evidence a network administrator would use to investigate misuse or diagnose connectivity issues.

8. Challenges Encountered

Windows server setup cannot find the microsoft software license terms, usually because the insallation media or ISO is corrupted, incomplete, or improperly mounted.

Ubuntus netplan apply fails because the YAML configuration has incorrect indentation. The error points specifically to via 192.168.10.1This one is an Ubuntu APT or network connection error

Ubuntu is trying to download package information from rchive.ubuntu.com and security.ubuntu.com

Temporary failure resolving- meaning the system cannot translate those domain names into ip addresss- usually a DNS or internet or network configuration problem.

As a result , some package index files could not be downloaded, so ubuntu may use older cached ones.
